To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a novel influenza virus ( H 10 ) was detected in the lung of a dead seal and was also found in 4 out of 6 seals with lung lesions.
a highly pathogenic avian influenza virus, H10N7, caused mass mortality of harbour seal ( Phoca vitu lina ) pups in Sweden in 2014.
the AIVs were detected in the lungs of 5 out of 6 dead seals and in one seal the AIV was also detected in the intestine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the investigation of the role of the novel avian influenza (AIV) A (H10N7) virus in the mass mortality events of harbour seals in the Swedish Baltic Sea.
the investigation of the involvement of avian influenza viruses in the 2014 mass mortality event in harbour seals ( Phocav itulina ).
the identification of the etiological agents responsible for mass mortality of harbour seal pups in Sweden in 2014.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the AIV H10N7 was involved in the mass mortality of the seals in Sweden.
the H 10 N7 influenza virus was the most probable causative agent for the mass mortality of seals in Sweden 2014.
the H 10 N7 avian influenza virus was the cause of mass mortality among the harbour seals in the Swedish Baltic Sea during 2014.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mass mortalities of harbour seals in Sweden during the summer 2014 were caused by an H10N7 avian influenza A virus.
the H 10 N7 virus, a reassortant of H 7 N 9 and H 10 N3 viruses, is the most likely candidate for the causative agent of the 2014 mass mortality of harbour seal in Sweden.
the H10N7 virus was detected in a few seals in March and April, but in a large proportion of the seals that were found dead in October.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the AIV (H10N7) virus is a novel pathogen in seals, and it has a potential to be a threat to the European seal populations.
the H10N7 virus was the likely cause of the 2014 mass mortality event of harbour seals in Sweden.
the H10N7 avian influenza virus is a potential threat to the health of harbour seals in Sweden and possibly elsewhere.
